newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian govt vows growth, urges calm over strikes.
newsitem.headline: Russian govt vows growth, urges calm over strikes.

text.p: Russia's new government brought in more liberal reformers in the final stage of a long reshuffle on Wednesday and committed itself to reviving the economy.

With the nation's patience wearing thin over billions of dollars of unpaid wages and pensions, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin appealed for more time and made a plea for calm during planned nationwide strikes and protests on Thursday.
"We mustn't get carried away be emotion and provocation," he said. "Such problems are not solved by demonstrations."
"We will do everything we can to resolve them," Chernomyrdin told a news conference after meeting President Boris Yeltsin to map the way forward and approve the latest cabinet appointees.
The new government's main and immediate target is to bring about economic growth and revive investment, the premier said.
"This is the task already for the current year," he said, stressing the need to begin radical structural reforms among companies, natural monopolies, housing and welfare.

In an effort to calm spirits, Chernomyrdin promised that the state and private employers would pay 11.8 trillion roubles ($2 billion) in back wages and pensions in March. The government puts total arrears at 53 trillion roubles.
It was not clear where the money would come from.
He stressed that tax collection was still the government's biggest headache and said sweeping reform of tax and budget policy was needed to keep state finances from seizing up.
Chernomyrdin, 58, was flanked by his youthful and reformist new first deputy prime minsters, Anatoly Chubais, 41, and Boris Nemtsov, 37. Both were appointed by Yeltsin earlier this month.

Maintaining the liberal tone of the president's reshaped team, Chernomyrdin said former economy minister Yevgeny Yasin, the guiding spirit of many Russian economic reforms would keep a government job as minister without portfolio, coordinating and reviewing economic policy.
Alexei Kudrin, a Chubais ally, became First Deputy Finance Minister. Chubais himself holds the finance portfolio.
Nemtsov said Yeltsin was determined to cut government spending.
Former governor of the carmaking region of Nizhny Novgorod, Nemtsov also said the state would no longer buy foreign cars.
He also said Yeltsin had promised to sign in three days a draft decree fighting corruption and boosting competition.

Chernomyrdin said he was aware of some plans to disrupt peaceful protests. The government has put security services on the alert. Trade unions say 20 million could turn out, although previous protests have failed to fire popular enthusiasm.
The leader of the extreme communist faction, Working Russia, forecast a "quiet and peaceful" day. Viktor Anpilov was quoted urging his supporters not to provoke disturbances.

Yeltsin demanded drastic changes in the government earlier this month. Returning to active politics after eight months of illness, the 66-year-old Kremlin leader acknowledged that his market reforms were failing to meet people's needs.

In an effort to halt the decline in incomes and free the economy from a web of corruption, organised crime and Soviet-style bureaucracy, he parachuted in his 41-year-old chief-of-staff Chubais to spearhead a new wave of reforms.

Last week, in an apparent effort to break a deadlock between Chubais and the more conservative Chernomyrdin, he also named Nemtsov, 37, a liberal regional governor, as a first deputy prime minister with a brief to crack down on monopolists.
